problems.problem_statement: Let a function be defined by \\(g(x) = \\int_{1}^{x^2} \\cos(\\pi t) \\, dt\\). Find the value of \\(g'(2)\\).
problems.solution: To find \\(g'(x)\\), we use the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part 2, combined with the Chain Rule. The theorem states that if \\(F(x) = \\int_{a(x)}^{b(x)} f(t) \\, dt\\), then \\(F'(x) = f(b(x)) \\cdot b'(x) - f(a(x)) \\cdot a'(x)\\).\\nFor the given function \\(g(x) = \\int_{1}^{x^2} \\cos(\\pi t) \\, dt\\), we have:\\n- \\(f(t) = \\cos(\\pi t)\\)\\n- The lower limit is a constant, \\(a(x) = 1\\), so \\(a'(x) = 0\\).\\n- The upper limit is a function of x, \\(b(x) = x^2\\), so \\(b'(x) = 2x\\).\\n\\nApplying the formula for \\(g'(x)\\):\\n\\(g'(x) = f(b(x)) \\cdot b'(x) - f(a(x)) \\cdot a'(x)\\)\\n\\(g'(x) = \\cos(\\pi (x^2)) \\cdot (2x) - \\cos(\\pi (1)) \\cdot (0)\\)\\n\\(g'(x) = 2x \\cos(\\pi x^2)\\)\\n\\nNow, we evaluate \\(g'(x)\\) at \\(x=2\\):\\n\\(g'(2) = 2(2) \\cos(\\pi (2^2))\\)\\n\\(g'(2) = 4 \\cos(4\\pi)\\)\\n\\nSince \\(\cos(2n\\pi) = 1\\) for any integer \\(n\\), we have \\(\cos(4\\pi) = 1\\).\\nTherefore:\\n\\(g'(2) = 4 \\cdot 1 = 4\\)

scaffolding.hint: Recall the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part 2. Since the upper limit of integration is \\(x^2\\) and not just \\(x\\), you will need to apply the Chain Rule.

Let \\(u = x^2\\). The derivative of \\(g(x)\\) with respect to \\(x\\) is given by \\(\frac{d}{dx} \\left[ \\int_{1}^{u} \\cos(\\pi t) \\, dt \\right] = \\left( \\frac{d}{du} \\int_{1}^{u} \\cos(\\pi t) \\, dt \\right) \\cdot \\frac{du}{dx}\\. Calculate this expression.
After finding the general expression for \\(g'(x)\\), substitute \\(x=2\\) and evaluate the result. Remember the value of \\(\cos(4\\pi)\\).
